analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set a stricter drinking water standard and health advisory for the solvent trichloroethylene.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: Rep. Hinchey introduced it with three Democratic cosponsors in March 2008, and it sat in committee until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Trichloroethylene (TCE) is a metal-degreasing solvent whose waste has contaminated over 1,000 waste sites nationwide, and whose vapors can seep from contaminated groundwater into homes. The bill would have directed the EPA, on fixed deadlines, to issue a health advisory and a national drinking water standard for TCE that protects pregnant women, infants, and children with a margin of safety, to require water systems to disclose TCE and its cancer risks in annual consumer reports, and to apply a protective vapor-intrusion standard at Superfund cleanup sites. It was introduced, referred to committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water or live near TCE-contaminated sites — the bill's own findings cite evidence linking TCE to kidney cancer and leukemia, and to birth defects from exposure in the womb. Water customers would also learn, through required consumer reports, whether TCE is in their water and what the cancer risks are for pregnant women and children.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families near TCE-contaminated water and sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA, within 180 days, to publish a health advisory for TCE in drinking water — including cancer risks — that fully protects susceptible populations (pregnant women, infants, and children) with an adequate margin of safety.

Requires EPA within 18 months to issue a binding national drinking water regulation for TCE, with the contaminant limit set as close to the health goal as feasible, and strengthens monitoring so systems near known contamination plumes cannot simply carry monitoring waivers.
Requires annual consumer confidence reports to disclose any TCE in drinking water and the health and cancer risks it poses to pregnant women, infants, and children.

Requires EPA to set a protective vapor-intrusion reference concentration and apply it at Superfund and other cleanup sites within two years, addressing TCE vapors migrating from groundwater and soil into indoor air — an exposure route that exists even where drinking water is unaffected.

analysis.who_pays: Water systems would bear new monitoring and, where limits tighten, treatment costs that get passed to ratepayers; industrial users of TCE — metal degreasers, adhesive and paint-remover makers — and parties responsible for contaminated Superfund sites would face stricter cleanup and compliance obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Water utilities, ratepayers, and TCE users

drawbacks.text: Tightening the drinking water limit would impose monitoring and treatment costs on public water systems, which pass those costs on to their customers as higher water rates — a real burden even for households far from any TCE plume.

The bill set hard statutory deadlines (180 days to 18 months) for EPA decisions, potentially faster than the agency's own scientific review process; the National Academy of Sciences report the bill itself cites recommended finalizing a risk assessment so risk decisions could be made expeditiously, and industry users would argue the timelines compressed that review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health protections are targeted at a contaminant the bill's own findings describe as the most frequently reported organic groundwater contaminant, with evidence of kidney cancer and leukemia risks strengthening since 2001, and with an existing limit (5 micrograms per liter) that EPA's own 2001 draft assessment suggested should be about 1. The costs fall on water systems and industrial users, partially passed to ratepayers, and the compressed deadlines are the most legitimate design criticism — but on the whole this is a straightforward public-health bill whose benefits would concentrate in contaminated communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to its environment subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the TCE Reduction Act of 2008 on March 4, 2008, joined by Reps. Hall of New York, Sestak, and Gillibrand.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died there when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill had only three cosponsors, all Democrats, and never attracted the broader support needed to move through committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water systems and industrial TCE users avoided new monitoring, treatment, and cleanup costs; communities drinking TCE-contaminated water, including pregnant women and children, got no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water systems and industrial TCE users

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered three Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. John Hall, Joe Sestak, and Kirsten Gillibrand

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the environment subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing or committee vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Industrial TCE users (metal degreasing, adhesives, paint removers)
industries.note: A tighter drinking water standard and Superfund vapor-intrusion limits would raise cleanup and compliance costs for businesses that use and discharge the solvent. Their avoiding those costs leaves the health burden of contamination with nearby residents.

Utilities would face revised monitoring requirements and, where TCE exceeds a new lower limit, treatment costs passed to ratepayers. But the bill also removes monitoring waivers near known contamination plumes, which means utilities near such sites would have to actually test for TCE.

industries.industry: Responsible parties at contaminated Superfund and waste sites
industries.note: Applying a protective vapor-intrusion reference concentration to Superfund and Safe Drinking Water Act cleanups would expand required remediation for parties on the hook for contamination sites.
